backups.overview: Mount Fairchild (6,899 ft) is the second-highest peak in the Bailey Range, a glaciated subrange deep in the interior of Olympic National Park's Daniel J. Evans Wilderness. It carries the small, retreating Fairchild Glacier on its northeast flank and sits about 0.84 mi northeast of higher neighbor Mount Carrie (6,995 ft). No trail comes anywhere close to the summit — nearly all ascents are made as a side-trip during the multi-day Bailey Range Traverse rather than as a standalone climb, and the peak sees only a handful of ascents most years. First climbed in 1963 by Denny Pruitt, Dan Baker, Jack Christiansen, and Roy Etten.
backups.beta: Mount Fairchild is the second-highest peak in the Bailey Range and is accessed via two primary routes: (1) the High Divide approach via Sol Duc and Mount Carrie, or (2) from the Elwha River over Mount Fitzhenry. Both routes involve significant glacier travel with crevasse hazards and require proper alpine mountaineering skills. The peak stands at the head of Fairchild Creek with the Fairchild Glacier on its east slope.
backups.turnaround: Firm turnaround; retreat options are limited
backups.permit: Olympic National Park: no permit for day climbs; all overnight wilderness stays require a wilderness camping permit via Recreation.gov.
backups.comms: No cell service anywhere in the Bailey Range or Olympic alpine backcountry. Satellite communicator (Garmin inReach or similar) essential for emergency communication. Contact Olympic National Park Wilderness Information Center at (360) 565-3100 before trip to file itinerary.
backups.descent: Descend via the standard descent route, retracing the ascent when possible. Be aware of loose rock and snow bridge hazards. Maintain group cohesion on exposed sections.

waypoints.name: Sol Duc Trailhead
waypoints.note: Large trailhead parking lot at the end of Sol Duc Hot Springs Road; Olympic National Park entrance pass required; overnight trips need a wilderness permit reserved in advance, since none are issued at the trailhead.
waypoints.directions: Turn south off US 101 onto Sol Duc Hot Springs Road (about 29 miles west of Port Angeles) and follow it, paved the whole way, past the park entrance station, the Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort and the campground to the large lot at road's end — the trailhead is at the very end, beyond the resort.

waypoints.name: Sol Duc Falls
waypoints.note: Trail crosses a footbridge just below the falls; last easy, reliable water before the climb toward Appleton Pass begins in earnest.
waypoints.directions: From the end of the lot take the Sol Duc River Trail up the valley: 0.8 mi of wide, near-level old-growth tread with essentially no elevation change (1,950 to 1,980 ft), ending at the footbridge just below the falls. This is the last easy, reliable water taken straight off the trail before the climbing starts.

waypoints.name: Appleton Pass Trail junction
waypoints.note: Leave the Sol Duc River Trail here and turn right/uphill onto the Appleton Pass Trail; elevation is a rough interpolation along the NPS-stated 2,000-5,100 ft climb.

waypoints.name: Appleton Pass
waypoints.note: Broad alpine pass on the Bailey Range crest with meadows and views into the Boulder Lake basin; leave the maintained trail here to begin cross-country travel into the Bailey Range proper.

waypoints.name: The Cat Walk (Cat Peak traverse)
waypoints.note: Old, narrow, exposed use-path sidehilling the steep flanks of Cat Peak; the steepest, most exposure-prone stretch of the whole approach, worse with a full pack.

waypoints.name: Boston Charlie's Camp
waypoints.note: Small flat tent spot at the east end of the Cat Walk with a shallow melt-water sinkhole pond; water needs filtering and the site is exposed to wind/weather.
waypoints.directions: Follow the sidehill path east to the far end of the Cat Walk arete, giving back roughly 200 ft. The camp is a single small flat tent spot at the east end with a shallow melt-water sinkhole pond beside it — filter that water, and expect the site to be fully exposed to wind and weather.

waypoints.name: Mount Carrie ridge/glacier gain
waypoints.note: Highest point in the Bailey Range (0.84 mi SW of Fairchild's summit); per the descent beta this is where the route regains the ridge/glacier system linking to the Fairchild Glacier.
waypoints.directions: Climb roughly 1,700 ft southeast from Boston Charlie's onto Mount Carrie (6,995 ft), the highest point in the Bailey Range. There is a real choice here: many parties sidehill the loose, exposed talus across Carrie's south face, but staying higher — up the ridge on Carrie's north side, over or just under the summit — avoids the worst of the sidehilling and sets up a cleaner entry onto the Fairchild Glacier. Where the crest becomes too sharp to walk, traverse up across the scree flanks. There is no reliable water on this stretch, so tank up at camp.

waypoints.name: Fairchild Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Rope up and don crampons/axe here; follow the wind-formed ridge down-glacier toward the exit col on Ruth Peak's shoulder — crevasse hazard, especially late season when snow bridges are thin.
waypoints.directions: Drop about 300 ft northeast off Carrie's ridge onto the upper Fairchild Glacier, which starts around 6,600-6,700 ft on the Bailey crest and falls away to the northeast. Rope up and put on crampons here; an ice axe is wanted most of the season. Rather than taking the direct line, follow the wind-formed snow ridge running down the glacier — the same idea as the Hogsback on Mount Hood — which keeps you clear of the crevasses. Late season the snow bridges thin and the surface goes to bare, hard ice, so this is full crampon technique, not microspikes.

waypoints.name: Mount Fairchild
waypoints.note: Second-highest peak in the Bailey Range; short final scramble on snow and rock from the glacier saddle to the true summit.
waypoints.directions: Leave the wind ridge and take the steeper exit section up onto Fairchild's summit ridge: roughly 35-40 degrees of snow past an icy patch, the steepest ground on the route. Stay roped and in crampons through it. From the summit ridge a short scramble on snow and rock gains the 6,899 ft true summit, second-highest in the Bailey Range. There is no rappel anywhere on this climb — the only way off is to reverse the entire line, and the glacier softens through the afternoon, so set an early turnaround.

backups.detailed_rack: Glacier kit for the Fairchild Glacier crossing; light gear for Class 2-3 rock
pro_tips: reserve your Olympic NP wilderness permit on Recreation.gov as soon as the summer release window opens (around mid-April) — walk-up availability for the Baileys is limited
a light glacier kit (short rope, tibloc/microtrax, a few slings) is usually sufficient for the short Fairchild/Carrie Glacier crossings rather than a full mountaineering rack
plan Fairchild as an add-on summit during a full Bailey Range Traverse itinerary rather than a standalone objective — nearly everyone who climbs it is already out there for the traverse
watch_out: snow bridges over crevasses on the Fairchild/Carrie Glaciers that look solid but are undercut, especially after mid-August

underestimating the time commitment — this is realistically a 3-5 day objective, not a long day trip, even for strong parties

backups.pro_needs: Glacier protection where snow/ice is present; minimal rock pro
backups.best_season: Mid-July through mid-August is the truly optimal window — snow bridges over crevasses are still generally intact and steep sidehill sections in the Northern Baileys have softened enough to travel safely. Conditions remain feasible into early September, but glaciers run increasingly bare and icy (full crampon use, not microspikes) and snow bridges become less reliable; earlier in July, persistent steep snow on the Northern Baileys traverses can make travel more hazardous.
backups.approach: There is no trail to Mount Fairchild itself, but the standard approach follows a well-defined maintained-trail corridor before turning to off-trail wilderness travel. Start at the Sol Duc River Trailhead (end of Sol Duc Road) on the Sol Duc River Trail. At 0.8 mi pass Sol Duc Falls, and at 0.9 mi reach the Lovers Lane junction; branch left onto the Deer Lake Trail, which climbs steeply and relentlessly through switchbacks to Deer Lake (3.4 mi, ~3,527 ft) — the first reliable water and the last easy camping before things get serious. Beyond Deer Lake the trail continues up through Potholes Meadows (~5 mi) and gains the High Divide ridge crest around 6 mi/4,730 ft, with good views and intermittent tarns/snowmelt for water. At 7.4 mi pass the Seven Lakes Basin junction (4,900 ft) — a good last water/camp option — then continue along High Divide past or near Bogachiel Peak (5,474 ft). At roughly 10.2 mi, leave the maintained trail system at the Cat Basin junction; from here it is off-trail cross-country and boot-path travel only, dropping into Cat Basin below Cat Peak (5,940 ft) and then crossing the Catwalk, the narrow, exposed class 3 ridge linking Cat Peak to Mount Carrie (6,995 ft). Past it, many parties use the exposed, loose-talus sidehill traverse across Carrie's south face; an alternative preferred by some climbers is to stay higher on Carrie's north side, which avoids the worst sidehilling and leads up Carrie's ridge and upper flanks to its summit. The route to Fairchild starts from Mount Carrie's summit: head northeast down the Carrie Glacier (rope up and put on crampons here; ice axe mandatory most of the season), circle around to the north of Fairchild, and climb its Southwest Ridge to the 6,899 ft summit. This final section is only thinly described, so expect to find the line yourself. One-way distance to this point is roughly 12 miles with substantial cumulative gain from repeated up-and-down over Bogachiel Peak, Cat Peak, and the Carrie ridge system, consistent with the ~8,000 ft round-trip gain. Hazards: early-season creek crossings near Sol Duc Falls, steep loose-scree switchbacks on the Deer Lake Trail, serious exposure and loose rock on the Catwalk traverse, crevasses and snow bridges on the Carrie Glacier requiring roped glacier travel (especially early/mid-summer), no reliable water between Cat Basin and the glacier, and heavy route-finding demands in fog/whiteout since the entire Cat Basin-to-summit section is unmarked wilderness travel.
backups.descent_text: This is a walk-off/glacier-descent route with no rappelling. Descend by reversing the ascent line: from the summit, descend the Southwest Ridge, circle back around the north side of the peak and reclimb the Carrie Glacier roped up with crampons to Mount Carrie's summit, then descend Mount Carrie's north-side ridge. Sidehill back across Carrie's south face (or take the north-side alternative), then recross the Catwalk to Cat Basin, drop to rejoin the maintained High Divide Trail at the Cat Basin junction (~10.2 mi mark), and retrace the trail past the Seven Lakes Basin junction, Bogachiel Peak, Potholes Meadows, Deer Lake, and Lovers Lane back down to Sol Duc Falls and the Sol Duc River Trailhead. Some parties instead continue the descent onward as part of the broader Bailey Range Traverse — dropping south past Ruth Peak toward Stephen Lake/Queets Basin and exiting via the Elwha (Whiskey Bend) or Hoh River trailheads — but that is a different, longer one-way multi-day itinerary rather than the out-and-back standard route matching this route's distance and gain. Descent hazards mirror the approach: crevasse fall potential on the glacier (softening snow in the afternoon raises post-holing/slot risk, so an early turnaround is wise), loose talus on the Carrie sidehill, fatigue-driven route-finding errors in the featureless heather and scree of Cat Basin, and long, tired-legs reversal of the steep Deer Lake Trail switchbacks.
backups.bail: Limited bail options - return along the approach

itinerary.cal: Best done mid-summer to early fall once the Long Creek ford is low and the glacier remnant is more open/less avalanche-prone; snow can linger on the approach ridges into July.

days.note: Start at the Whiskey Bend trailhead and follow the Elwha River Trail roughly 2 miles to Michaels Ranch, then turn onto the Long Ridge Trail, crossing the Elwha on a high suspension bridge before climbing steadily through forest onto the ridge. This maintained trail section gains several thousand feet and is the last easy walking of the trip.

From there climb steep, mossy, brushy slopes to a high camp near timberline below Fitzhenry.

access.fees: $8 per adult (16+) per night backcountry camping fee plus a non-refundable $6 reservation fee per permit, or a $45 Annual Olympic Wilderness Pass (reservation fee still applies); standard park entrance fee also applies for vehicle access.
access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: Bear canisters are mandatory for all overnight off-trail camping in the Bailey Range.
access.permit: NPS wilderness camping permit required for any overnight stay in the Bailey Range; reserve on Recreation.gov (summer-season permits typically release around mid-April) or through the Wilderness Information Center, (360) 565-3100.
access.closures: Sol Duc Road closes seasonally in winter/early spring — check the NPS road-conditions line (360-565-3131) or nps.gov/olym road-conditions page before driving in. The Bailey Range route itself is generally only safely passable from roughly July through September.

climate.fall: Conditions deteriorate quickly after mid-September with increasing rain, wind, and early snow.
climate.spring: Heavy snowpack lingers into early summer; the Catwalk and glacier crossing are typically not viable until snow consolidates.
climate.summer: July-September is the reliable weather and access window, though rain and wind can still arrive with little warning.
climate.winter: Not a winter objective — access roads close seasonally and the range holds a deep, unstable snowpack.
climate.typical: The Bailey Range interior sees more precipitation and cloud cover than the rain-shadow towns north of the park but less than the drenched western river valleys; persistent snowfields commonly linger into July even in average years.

bySeason.summer: Prime climbing window mid-July through early September; best conditions (intact snow bridges, softer sidehill snow) are mid-July to mid-August.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC issues an 'Olympics' avalanche/mountain-weather zone forecast, but NWAC only operates in winter (roughly mid-November through mid-April) — for summer climbing conditions, use NWS point forecasts for the area plus recent trip reports.

emergency.notes: No cell coverage anywhere in the Bailey Range interior; carry a satellite communicator (inReach/SPOT). Serious trauma cases are typically evacuated by helicopter (Olympic NP SAR / Airlift Northwest) to Harborview Medical Center in Seattle.
emergency.rangerStation: Olympic National Park Wilderness Information Center (Port Angeles), (360) 565-3100
emergency.nearestHospital: Olympic Medical Center (Olympic Memorial Hospital), 939 Caroline St, Port Angeles — roughly 2+ hours' drive from the Sol Duc Trailhead, considerably farther from interior camps

crowds.peakTraffic: Rare even in peak summer (late July-August); trip reports on the Bailey Range consistently describe seeing few or no other parties once past the Sol Duc/Cat Walk approach, though the approach trails themselves (Sol Duc past Heart Lake, Sol Duc Falls) see real hiker/tourist traffic
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Very low - likely well under 20 parties per season summit Fairchild itself; it's usually a side-objective off the Bailey Range Traverse rather than a standalone destination

fitnessSpec.hiking: Very high - the approach is a multi-day (often 5-8 day) largely off-trail traverse or long valley approach with sustained brush, talus, and elevation gain/loss before Fairchild is even reached
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Heavy expedition pack (roughly 40-50+ lbs with food/fuel for a week), sustained over rugged, unmaintained terrain

partner_requirements.approachTime: Multi-day - typically several days of travel (via the Bailey Range Traverse or long approaches from Sol Duc/Hoh) to reach a high camp before the final scramble to the summit, consistent with the 12-hour summit-day timing estimate starting from high camp
requiredSkills: Off-trail route-finding and navigation in complex, unmarked terrain (map/compass or GPS, not just trail-following)
Snowfield travel and self-arrest with an ice axe
Roped glacier travel and crevasse rescue for the Fairchild Glacier crossing
Multi-day backcountry self-sufficiency (route selection, water/camp logistics, weather judgment) given the remoteness
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Seasoned off-trail mountaineer/scrambler with multi-day wilderness expedition experience; this is not a route for someone whose only background is trail hiking or single-day scrambles

July.reason: Early July can still carry heavy lingering snowpack ('heavy lingering snow; avalanche hazard' in spring bleeding into early summer); conditions generally improve and firm up by mid-to-late July

August.reason: The best window - snow has cleared from most of the route and the long approach is most reliable

September.reason: Still climbable in early September, but with shortening days and early storm possibility, which is a real concern this far from an escape route

weather.typical: Interior Olympics climate: heavy winter snowpack with long approaches; best window is mid-July through early September once snow clears
weather.probability: Pacific frontal systems can bring sudden weather changes even in summer, and early storms are a fall risk; with the remoteness, there is very limited escape if weather turns

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Technically moderate (Class 2-3), but consequence is high: this is one of the most remote objectives in the range, with a long, committing approach and essentially no quick escape or rescue option if something goes wrong above high camp

avalanche.zone: No NWAC forecast zone provides operational coverage of this route - NWAC's Olympics-area forecasting is issued only in the winter/spring backcountry ski season and does not run during the July-September climbing window for this route

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: Real - the line drops from Mount Carrie onto the Fairchild Glacier, which has open crevasses beside its snow ridge and turns to hard blue ice late in the season; hidden crevasses are likelier early, before the snow consolidates, so travel roped

approach_variants.name: High Divide and Cat Basin to the Fairchild Glacier
approach_variants.notes: Sol Duc to Deer Lake, up through Potholes Meadows onto the High Divide crest and past Bogachiel Peak, leaving maintained trail at the Cat Basin junction around ten miles. From there it is boot path and cross-country below Cat Peak and around Mount Carrie. Almost every ascent happens mid-traverse rather than as a standalone climb.
hazards: Crevasses and thin snow bridges on the Fairchild Glacier, worse late season
Bare, hard glacier ice by late summer needing full crampon technique
Severe exposure and loose talus on the sidehill traverse across Carrie
No dependable water between Cat Basin and the glacier
Route-finding across largely featureless post-glacial ground in whiteout
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base here is a glacier entry rather than a rock step, and the marker is a snow feature. From Cat Basin, climb or sidehill around Mount Carrie — the higher line on Carrie's north side avoids the worst of the traverse and sets up a cleaner entry than the exposed sidehill does. Aim to reach the upper Fairchild Glacier at roughly 6,700 ft on the northeast side of the Carrie–Fairchild ridge. You are in the right place when a wind-formed snow ridge runs away down the glacier ahead of you: a firm raised spine, much like a hogsback, and it exists precisely because following it keeps you clear of the crevassed ground on either side. Rope up and put crampons on before stepping onto it, not once you are committed. Lower, flatter snow aprons on the same flank look like easier entries and lead into broken ice, so do not take the first snow you meet. Near the summit ridge the spine steepens to something like 35 to 40 degrees beside an icy patch — that is the correct exit rather than a sign you are off line. Bare rock and moraine underfoot means you are still below the glacier.

bivy.name: Eleven Bull Basin and the Cream Lake cross-country camps
bivy.notes: These are the working camps for Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild. Eleven Bull Basin sits beneath Carrie and Ruth, a meadow with running streams, and it is the natural second night for a party that climbed Carrie from Boston Charlie's. Fairchild is the next peak along the crest, less than a mile north of Ruth, and both are class 3 from this side. Beyond, the route continues toward Ferry Basin and eventually Glacier Pass, which is the only way Mount Mathias is reached from this end — several more days of committing off-trail travel, some of it on glacier. Water dictates the itinerary here far more than distance does, so plan camps around the basins rather than around mileage.
bivy.water: Good in Eleven Bull Basin, where streams run out of the hillside most of the season; sparse between there and Cream Lake, and Cream Lake itself is swampy and buggy enough that many parties take the higher bypass toward Stephen Lake instead
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, arranged by phone with the park's wilderness information office — these are not campsites you can pick off the online map. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned, and the leave-no-trace expectation is stricter here than at any designated camp because nothing is hardened.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed cross-country camping in meadow basins; no designated sites, no toilets, and no capacity beyond what the ground will take without damage

bivy.name: Cat Basin
bivy.notes: Cat Basin lies just below the junction at roughly 5,042 ft where the High Divide trail meets the way into the Bailey Range, so it is the last sheltered ground on the approach before the route turns cross-country beneath Cat Peak. Parties heading for Mount Carrie use it to shorten the following morning and to get below the wind, since the divide itself is fully exposed. It is genuinely primitive — expect to be finding your own flat spot on durable ground, and expect the sites to be scattered rather than obvious. In heavy snow years the basin fills late and the traverse out to the Catwalk holds steep snow well into July.
bivy.water: Streams in the basin early in the season, unreliable by late summer; carry from Heart Lake if the year has been dry
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required. This one is worth phoning the park's wilderness information office about rather than assuming — the primitive and cross-country parts of this area are not all bookable through the standard online map, and staff issue those permits directly. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned outright at this height.
bivy.capacity: A primitive designated area rather than a developed camp; a handful of tent spots, no toilet you should count on

bivy.name: Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort campground
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging base for every objective in this zone except Mount Angeles, a couple of miles short of the end of the Sol Duc Hot Springs Road where the trailhead for the High Divide and Appleton Pass sits. Climbers use it the night before, because the walk to Heart Lake or Appleton Pass is long enough that leaving Port Angeles in the morning wastes the day. It opens with the season, roughly late March into late October, and it fills solidly on summer weekends. It is a staging base and nothing more — from here you still have the entire approach ahead of you, and every camp above it is permit-controlled.
bivy.water: Potable water and flush toilets in the comfort stations through the operating season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — this is a frontcountry campground with a nightly fee, taken on the federal recreation booking site or through the resort. Park entrance fee applies. Fires are allowed in the provided rings here, unlike anywhere you are going above it.
bivy.capacity: Around 82 tent sites plus a smaller RV loop; most tent sites are reservable and a handful are held back first-come

bivy.name: Deer Lake
bivy.notes: Three and a half miles up from the Sol Duc trailhead by way of Sol Duc Falls, this is the first camp on the loop and the one parties take when they get away late and cannot face the climb to Heart Lake in the dark. For a Bailey Range objective it is a poor base on its own — you are still well below the High Divide and four or more miles short of where the cross-country travel starts — so treat it as a way of splitting the walk in rather than as a summit camp. Its low elevation and lake make it the most forgiving camp in the zone in bad weather, and it holds snow later into the spring than its height suggests.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus Canyon Creek on the way up; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and this is a QUOTA camp reserved for a specific night on the federal booking site. Approved bear canisters are mandatory throughout the Sol Duc, High Divide and Seven Lakes Basin area. Campfires are banned — nothing above 3,500 ft in this park may have one, and this camp sits right at that line.
bivy.capacity: A modest cluster of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; parties of seven or more must use a designated group site

bivy.name: Heart Lake
bivy.notes: The most useful camp in the whole zone for a climber. It sits just under eight miles in, a short climb below the High Divide, and it is the last camp on maintained trail with easy water before the route to Mount Carrie, Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild leaves the trail for good. From here you gain the divide, follow it past Cat Peak, cross the exposed class 3 ridge known as the Catwalk, and the climbing starts. Parties who miss the permit sometimes take a Seven Lakes Basin camp such as Lunch Lake instead, but that puts you off the direct line and adds side-hilling in the morning. Fill every bottle here — the stretch from the divide out to the first Bailey Range camps carries no running water.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake and the creek feeding it, all season; this is the last dependable running water for a long way
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, QUOTA camp booked for a specific night on the federal booking site. Reservations for the summer season open in the spring and the High Divide camps are among the fastest to go in the park, often within minutes. Bear canisters mandatory, no campfires.
bivy.capacity: A small number of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; group parties must use the designated group site

bivy.name: Boston Charlie's Camp
bivy.notes: This is the first camp on the far side of the Catwalk and the recognised start of the Bailey Range proper. It matters because it puts you directly at the foot of Mount Carrie's southwest ridge, where the route gains around 2,000 ft in under a mile on a semi-cairned bootpack, so a party camped here can be on the summit early and off the loose ground before the afternoon. Getting to it means crossing the exposed class 3 ridge between Cat Peak and Carrie with a full pack, which is the crux of the approach for most people and not somewhere to be in wet weather. The water is the honest drawback and the reason some parties push straight through to the basins beyond.
bivy.water: Poor and the standing complaint about the place — a shallow sinkhole pond that is often silty and stagnant, and nothing else nearby. Filter and treat, and consider carrying from Heart Lake or Cat Basin
bivy.permit: Covered by an Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, which for the Bailey Range is arranged directly with the park's wilderness information office rather than booked as a named campsite online. Bear canisters mandatory. No fires. Camp on durable surfaces — snow, rock or gravel — and pack out everything.
bivy.capacity: Informal cross-country bivy sites for a couple of small parties; no facilities of any kind

backups.overview: Lost Peak (8,464 ft, 1,624 ft prominence) sits in the Okanogan Range of the North Cascades, about 16 miles north of Mazama and 7 miles northwest of Big Craggy Peak, deep in the interior of the Pasayten Wilderness. It ranks among Washington's 100 highest peaks. There is no trail to the summit — it lies several cross-country miles beyond the nearest maintained trail, so most parties combine it with nearby Pass Butte and/or the Lago group (Mt. Lago, Mt. Carru, Osceola Peak, Blackcap Peak) on a multi-day loop rather than climbing it in isolation. Lage Wernstedt, the USFS topographer credited with numerous early Pasayten first ascents (nearby Dot Mountain is named for his wife, Dottie), is credited with the first ascent in 1925.
backups.beta: Lost Peak has no technical climbing routes. The standard (and essentially only documented) line ascends loose scree/talus on the southwest slope at Class 3. Parties approaching from the north often traverse in from Pass Butte along the connecting ridge/slopes to avoid the worst of the scree found on the south and southwest aspects, then descend via the southwest slope/ridge. Because the approach is 20+ miles round trip through unmaintained trail on parts of the route, most parties treat this as a 3-day wilderness backpack rather than a day climb.
backups.turnaround: Set a hard summit-day turnaround (e.g., early afternoon): the ridge above Butte Pass has no shelter from thunderstorms, and finding the way back to camp through cross-country terrain is much harder in fog, dark, or storm.
backups.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass at some trailheads.
backups.comms: No reliable cell coverage in this part of the Pasayten Wilderness backcountry; a satellite messenger (inReach/SPOT) is recommended for the multi-day approach.
backups.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line off the summit via the southwest/northwest ridge, down loose talus and scree back to Butte Pass or the North Monument Creek basin, then retrace the multi-day approach trail out. No rappels are required on the standard scramble route; the main descent hazard is controlling scree underfoot and avoiding rockfall onto party members below.
obj_haz: early/late-season snow and possible cornices on north-facing gullies
swift snowmelt fords of North Monument Creek and Eureka Creek
afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter above treeline
remote self-rescue distance — multi-day from any trailhead or road

waypoints.name: Monument Creek Trailhead (Lost River Road / Harts Pass Road)
waypoints.note: USFS trailhead on Lost River Road (FR 5400 spur); no parking pass needed; fill out the free self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk, last reliable water/toilet before miles of Pasayten trail.

waypoints.name: Robinson Pass
waypoints.note: Gains the Middle Fork Pasayten divide via a steep final 1.2-mile forested pitch; trail forks here toward the Pasayten River valley.
waypoints.directions: Trail #478 follows Robinson Creek through big timber for about six miles, never far from the sound of the water, then fords the creek. Above the ford the grade stays gradual through forest, crossing several avalanche runouts, and breaks into meadowland near 4,700 ft. Pass the Slate Pass Trail junction and finish with a half mile of open meadow climbing to the pass.

waypoints.name: Middle Fork Pasayten River flats
waypoints.note: Common first-night camp beside the river a few miles below Robinson Pass; reliable water but mosquito-heavy in early season.
waypoints.directions: Drop off the far side of the pass and descend about three miles into the broad U-shaped Middle Fork valley, losing roughly 1,800 ft to river level. Camps sit along the water here.

waypoints.name: Fred's Lake
waypoints.note: Green alpine lake ringed by larches with a popular established camp; last dependable water before the Rolo/Shellrock high country.
waypoints.directions: Continue down-river before the trail turns and climbs back into the high country, gaining around 2,100 ft to the lake basin. Fred's Lake sits a short way off the main trail rather than on it, so watch for the spur or you will walk straight past it.

waypoints.name: Rolo Pass
waypoints.note: Ridge-crest pass just above Fred's Lake; route continues cross-country toward the head of Eureka Creek and Shellrock Basin.
waypoints.directions: From the lake keep climbing to the ridge-crest pass a few hundred feet above, through open larch and talus. The maintained tread thins out above the lake, and this is where the route stops being a trail hike.

waypoints.name: Shellrock Pass / Shellrock Basin
waypoints.note: Trail here has been unmaintained for decades and the basin fogs in frequently; easy to lose the faint tread in whiteout, navigate by map/compass.
waypoints.directions: From Rolo Pass drop to the headwaters of Eureka Creek and traverse across into Shellrock Basin, then climb to the pass at 7,500 ft. The tread through here has been unmaintained for decades and is faint to nonexistent, and the basin fogs in readily — carry map and compass and be ready to navigate without seeing any of the surrounding peaks.

waypoints.name: Lost Peak
waypoints.note: Class 3 talus/meadow scramble up the southwest or northwest ridge from a Shellrock Pass area camp; descend the same ridge line reversed.
waypoints.directions: From a camp near the pass, gain either the southwest or the northwest ridge and follow it over talus and alpine meadow to the top. Class 3 with no sustained technical ground, but the crest is high, exposed to wind, and can hold snow well past midsummer.

what_to_bring: free self-issue wilderness permit (fill out at the trailhead register)
topo map + compass or GPS/inReach — much of the route is cross-country with no trail

backups.pro_needs: Easy class 2 scramble; no technical gear normally required.
backups.best_season: Mid-July through September. Snow lingers on north-facing terrain and passes into early-mid July in an average year; one late-September (9/22-9/26) party found the high ridges around Lost Peak snowy, cold, and wind-blasted, with early-season alpine conditions, so shoulder-season parties should be ready for winter-like weather above treeline.
backups.approach: Lost Peak sits deep in the Pasayten Wilderness and the standard approach is a serious backcountry undertaking, not a day hike from a roadside trailhead. From the Monument Creek Trailhead (2,400 ft, off Lost River Road) follow Monument Creek Trail #484, which is well-maintained through old-growth forest for the first ~4 miles along Monument Creek and the Lost River — water is plentiful here and this stretch is even rideable by mountain bike, which some parties use to bank easy miles before caching bikes at the wilderness boundary. At roughly mile 4 the maintained tread ends at a washed-out bridge over Eureka Creek; beyond this point the trail has not been maintained in 25-30 years and becomes a faint, brushy, deadfall-choked route requiring solid navigation and a ford of Eureka Creek. Continue up the Monument Creek drainage (on-and-off tread, increasingly cross-country) into the North Monument Creek basin, where parties commonly camp at a small pond/tarn below Butte Pass — this is roughly 16+ miles in and the practical base camp for the peak (an alternate approach comes in from Robinson Creek/Shellrock Pass to the south, about 21.5 miles, used on longer Pasayten-Eleven traverses). From camp, climb to Butte Pass, then follow the ridge directly up to Pass Butte (~8,140 ft). From Pass Butte, continue along the connecting ridge over the col near Point 8107 and southeast across several false summits — Class 2 talus and rock scrambling, reported as 'quite fun' underfoot with mostly firm dirt/talus rather than loose scree — to Lost Peak's summit. Given the recorded ~77 km round-trip distance, this route is essentially always done as a multi-day backpack with the peak tagged as a day-scramble from high camp, not car-to-car. Hazards: the unmarked, unmaintained trail beyond Eureka Creek with brush and deadfall; the Eureka Creek ford; remote terrain with no cell coverage; a long, navigation-heavy ridge walk with numerous false summits that is easy to get wrong in poor visibility; and lingering snow or sudden weather on the high, exposed ridge even in summer.
backups.descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble descent with no rappelling — reverse the Class 2 ridge scramble back over the false summits to the col near Point 8107, back along the connecting ridge to Pass Butte, and down to Butte Pass and camp. At least one documented party descended via a west-ridge variant instead of a strict reversal while staying in radio contact with other group members, so there is some flexibility in the exact line off the summit ridge, but no technical gear or fixed anchors are involved either way. The main descent hazards are the same navigation difficulty as the ascent — multiple false summits and a broad ridge crest that can be disorienting in whiteout, wind, or after dark (one party topped out near 8:45 PM and descended by headlamp) — plus the standard alpine risks of afternoon thunderstorms and residual snow patches on the exposed ridge. From camp, the return to the trailhead simply reverses the ~16+ mile approach down Monument Creek, re-fording Eureka Creek and picking the maintained tread back up for the final 4 miles to the trailhead.
backups.bail: The standard route has no technical downclimbing or rappels, so bailing off the peak itself is straightforward in good weather. The real commitment is the multi-day cross-country approach — retreating from deep in the North Monument Creek/Shellrock Pass basin in bad weather is slow, so build in extra food/fuel days rather than pushing a closing weather window.

pitch_detail.notes: Multi-day trail approach (roughly 9-11+ miles one-way over Robinson Pass or to Pistol Pass, depending on trailhead) including unmaintained trail sections and an Eureka Creek ford, to a high camp near Butte Pass or Shellrock Pass.
Loose scree/talus scramble up the southwest slope to the 8,464-ft summit; often linked with Pass Butte via a connecting ridge traverse from the north.

Separately, the Ptarmigan Fire closure (Forest Service order 06-17-04-26-39, in effect September 9 through October 31, 2026) closes Monument Creek Trail #484 north of the Lake of the Woods turnoff, Eureka Creek Trail #474, Robinson Creek Trail #478 north of Eureka Creek, and Buckskin Ridge Trail #498; Methow Valley Ranger District, (509) 996-4000. Verify current status with the Methow Valley Ranger District before planning a trip.

climate.fall: Cool and often clear, with larch color in nearby basins by late September, but increasing chance of early-season snow.
climate.spring: Snowbound through at least June at these elevations; access road/trails typically not clear until late June.
climate.summer: Warm to hot days with cool nights; afternoon thunderstorms are common in the high country.
climate.winter: Heavy snow and cold; the peak and access roads are effectively inaccessible.
climate.typical: Dry, sunnier east-slope-Cascades climate compared to the west side, but still exposed and cold at elevation — expect cold nights and possible summer thunderstorms even in August. Snow can linger on north aspects and passes into early-mid July.

bySeason.fall: Larches turn gold in Eureka Creek/Shellrock Basin in late September, but a documented late-Sept trip found the high ridges already "snowy, cold, and wind-blasted" — treat late season as shoulder winter conditions.
bySeason.spring: Passes and approach trails are typically snow-covered and not practical for this route.
bySeason.summer: Late July through September is the reliable snow-free window for the high passes (Rolo, Shellrock, Butte); a normal winter clears most routes by early-mid July.
bySeason.winter: Not a winter objective — Harts Pass Road and interior trails are snowbound and the wilderness is essentially inaccessible.

approach_variants.name: Butte Pass, Pass Butte and the connecting ridge
approach_variants.notes: Lost Peak sits several cross-country miles beyond the end of any maintained trail and is normally a three-day trip rather than a climb. The common line follows the Monument Creek trail, which is well graded and even rideable by bike for the first few miles along the creek and the Lost River, then ends abruptly at a washed-out bridge; beyond that the tread has been unmaintained for decades and is faint, brushy and choked with deadfall. Parties camp at a small pond below Butte Pass in the North Monument Creek basin. A longer line comes in from the Robinson Creek side over Shellrock Pass and is used on extended traverses. The climbing is genuinely easy; the navigation over a long ridge of false summits is not.

A long ridge of false summits, disorienting in whiteout or after dark
Cross-country travel above the passes with no trail and no cairns

Afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter above treeline
Multi-day self-rescue distance from any road
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base is Butte Pass and the rise immediately above it. From the pond camp in the North Monument Creek basin, climb to the pass; the ridge running directly up out of it to Pass Butte, around 8,140 ft, is the start of the route, and Pass Butte is the first thing on the day you actually have to climb rather than walk to. Reaching its top is the confirmation, because from there the rest of the mountain lays out in front of you: a connecting ridge running southeast over a col near Point 8107 and on across a run of rises to Lost Peak. Underfoot is the second confirmation and a reassuring one, since the ridge line is mostly firm dirt and blocky talus that takes an edge, quite unlike the ball-bearing scree found on the south and southwest aspects of the peak. If the ground has gone to sliding scree you have dropped off the crest onto a flank. The real problem here is not finding the start but knowing when you have finished. The ridge throws up several rises that each look final from the one before, and nothing on it is the summit until the ground simply stops climbing to the southeast; budget for more than one disappointment and do not commit to a descent line off what you think is the top until you can see the ridge continuing no higher. Parties coming from the north sometimes traverse in across Pass Butte's slopes to stay off the loose southern aspects entirely, which is the same start by a slightly higher line.

bivy.name: Dot Lake and the Butte Pass basins — the far end of the traverse for Lost Peak
bivy.notes: LOST PEAK at 8,464 ft sits at the eastern end of this group between Monument Creek and the Lost River, and it is the awkward one — it does not fall out of a Carru and Lago camp the way those two fall out of each other. From the Shellrock country the usual line descends to Dot Lake, crosses a burned basin to Butte Pass and then works along a ridge with several false summits before the true top, which is a long day and one that parties routinely finish late. Camping at the lake rather than pushing back over Lago is what makes it sane, and it is the specific advice most trip accounts give: do not retrace the ridge, drop and camp. The alternative approach from the Monument Creek trailhead up the Lost River is a different trip entirely and its camps are covered in the Harts Pass file. Reckon on four days minimum for a party collecting Lost with the others, and note that the burn through here is extensive enough that navigation is easy and shade is nonexistent. Late July through September, and later is better for the passes.
bivy.water: Dot Lake is the dependable one and the reason to camp here rather than on the ridge. The basins beyond it toward Butte Pass are dry once the snow goes, and much of the ground between has burned, which makes the shade and the seeps both unreliable. Fill at the lake.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Slate Pass, Robinson Creek or Monument Creek depending on which end you started. Camp back from the shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock, no tying animals to trees. Fires legal outside a ban but there is little to burn and the ground is fragile.
bivy.capacity: Informal ground around the lake and in the basins toward the pass, room for a party or two. Nothing developed, nothing signed, and you will almost certainly be alone.

bivy.name: The Berk Creek junction and the Middle Fork Pasayten river camps
bivy.notes: This is the hinge of the whole Middle Fork approach and it is where a party bound for MOUNT CARRU, MOUNT LAGO or LOST PEAK actually sleeps on the first night. Two roads reach it: the high start from Slate Pass at nearly 6,900 ft with a short connector down to the Middle Fork trail, or the low start from the Robinson Creek trailhead at about 2,560 ft over Robinson Pass at 6,220 ft, which is nine and a half miles before the valley walking even begins. The high start is shorter by a long way and is what most parties use. From the junction the climb to Freds Pass and the crossing of the upper Eureka Creek country puts you in position for the summits; the whole approach from a road is around fifteen miles. Being on the river rather than up at the lakes costs you height on the second day and buys you shelter, running water and a warmer night — a real trade when the high camps are exposed and dry. The forest here is patchy burn in places and blowdown varies. This is remote country by any standard and there is no mobile service anywhere in the valley.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Middle Fork Pasayten and Berk Creek meet here and both run all season. This is the last easy water before the long climb to the passes, and the country above lives on tarns and snowmelt, so fill completely.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Slate Pass or Robinson Creek, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, though the valley is dry and bans are common by August.
bivy.capacity: A single established site at the junction where the trail up to Freds Lake and Doris Lake leaves the Middle Fork, plus scattered ground along the river flats above and below it. One or two parties each, nothing developed.

bivy.name: The high bench southwest of Shellrock Pass
bivy.notes: This is the staging camp that makes MOUNT CARRU and MOUNT LAGO short days instead of enormous ones, and it is deliberately not the same ground as the Shellrock Basin and Eureka Creek meadow camps lower down. It is a bench at around 7,500 ft immediately southwest of the pass, high enough that every summit in the group is within reach from it. For Carru the line runs west along the east fork of Eureka Creek, leaves the trail at a creek crossing and takes a red talus gully east of the Carru-Lago saddle for a few hundred feet — under two hours from camp to the 8,595 ft summit. Lago at 8,745 ft is the highest thing in this part of the wilderness and goes from the same saddle. WHAT YOU PAY FOR THE POSITION IS WATER AND WEATHER. There is no tree cover, the pass funnels wind, and a party that has not carried enough will be walking back down for it. Snow holds on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the real constraint on when this is worth doing. Larches turn in the last days of September and the nights at this height are properly cold by then.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and a small tarn below the pass, both of them seasonal. By late summer there may be nothing at all up here and the passes on either side are reliably dry. Carry water up from the Eureka Creek meadows or the river; this is the single most common mistake made on these summits.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass to park. The bench is thin alpine ground that holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the turf alone. Assume no fires — there is nothing to burn at this elevation and the meadows below are fragile.
bivy.capacity: Roughly half an acre of usable bench, so realistically two or three small parties. No established sites, no facilities and no shelter of any kind.

backups.overview: Mount Ballard is a remote, double-summit peak sharing a long ridgeline with its higher neighbor Azurite Peak, near the head of Mill Creek and about 2 miles north of Azurite Peak. It ranks 84th on Washington's 100 highest peaks and rises about 4,000 ft above Mill Creek within roughly a mile, giving it dramatic local relief despite being a non-technical scramble. A 2023 precision survey found the true summit lies about 1,100 ft south of, and higher than, the point long mapped/benchmarked as 'Mount Ballard' (8,301 ft), which is actually a lower north sub-summit. There is no maintained trail to the top; all routes leave trail well below the summit to scramble broad talus, heather, and gully terrain.
backups.beta: From Harts Pass Road, descend into the South Fork Slate Creek drainage, cross the South Fork on a metal bridge, and traverse open forest to a basin around 4,900 ft. From there climb through trees and open slopes to a bench on the east ridge (~6,200 ft), then continue up mixed class 3-4 rock and steep snow (up to 45-50°), angling left through cliff bands to reach the upper east ridge (~7,650 ft). At the col below the summit, cross a snow-covered ledge on the west face to the base of the summit gully, then scramble a short class 3-4 section, a ~10 ft class 4 corner, and blocky class 3 terrain to the true south summit. Parties describe route-finding through the cliff bands as the crux of navigation, and the final summit block as the technical crux (brief low 5th class, per one party).
backups.turnaround: There is no fixed clock-time turnaround — the approach is long (documented round trips of 8.5-10 hours) and includes route-finding through cliff bands and steep snow. Set a turnaround based on remaining daylight, weather trends, and snow condition: wet, sun-softened snow on the 45-50° slopes sharply increases fall risk, and if the col/summit gully hasn't been reached with enough daylight and stable snow remaining to retrace the route, retreat.
backups.face: East Ridge (Slate Creek approach) with a West Face finish to the true summit
backups.permit: No wilderness permit applies - Mount Ballard is on Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest land and is not within the Pasayten Wilderness. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at some trailheads.
backups.descent: Descend the same broad south-facing slopes/gully used on the ascent back down to the basin above the Azurite Mine (~6,600 ft); the scree and talus are loose, so downclimb carefully and avoid being directly above other climbers to prevent knocking rock onto them. From the basin, reverse whichever approach was used (Mill Creek Trail, or Mill Creek plus West Fork Methow River Trail/PCT) back to the trailhead — the lower, brush-choked stretch of the Mill Creek Trail is typically as slow going out as coming in.

backups.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the standard route. Bring an ice axe and crampons for the steep (up to 45-50°) snowfields below the col, which can persist well into summer. A single short rope with a few slings can be carried to protect the brief low 5th-class/exposed class 4 step near the true summit for less experienced or larger parties, though most parties free-solo it.
pro_tips: Combine with Azurite from a shared high camp
Stay on firmer rock to avoid loose scree near the top
backups.pro_needs: No fixed protection (bolts or pitons) exists on the route — it's a scramble with one short, exposed low-5th-class move near the summit. Any belay on that step would be improvised off natural rock features.
backups.approach: Standard approach: drive Highway 20 to the Canyon Creek Trailhead near milepost 141, west of Rainy Pass and follow the Mill Creek/Azurite Pass Trail (#755) up Canyon Creek then Mill Creek — about 11 miles (roughly 6 along Canyon Creek, then 5 up Mill Creek) to the site of the defunct Azurite Mine, then a further ~3 increasingly faint, brush-choked miles (slide alder and downed timber are common since the trail has seen little maintenance since the mine closed) to roughly the 14-mile mark, where a boot path continues about 1.5 more miles to Azurite Pass (6,680+ ft). A longer alternate, more often used for combined Azurite-Ballard trips, starts at the West Fork Methow River Trailhead (#480) near River Bend Campground: follow that trail ~8 miles to the PCT, then the PCT south ~1.5 miles to Horse Heaven Camp before joining the Mill Creek Trail to the pass — this option runs closer to 25 miles round trip with about 6,000 ft of elevation gain.
backups.descent_text: Descend the south slopes, retracing the ascent into the basin.
backups.bail: Reverse the scramble; no fixed anchors required.

pitch_detail.notes: Old road/forest traverse from Slate Creek Road gate, over the South Fork bridge, to the ~4,900 ft basin.
Ascend snow/rock from the 4,900 ft basin to a 6,200 ft bench, then continue to ~7,650 ft, angling left through cliff bands; slopes up to 45-50°.
Traverse a snow-covered ledge on the west face to the summit gully; finish with a ~10 ft class 4 corner and short class 3 blocks to the true (south) summit.

itinerary.cal: The Mill Creek Trail is severely brushed-in and essentially unmaintained year-round, so most parties wait until after peak snowmelt (mid-July through September) to reduce stream crossings and lingering snow on the upper mountain.

days.note: Hike the Canyon Creek Trail (about 6 good miles) then turn onto the Mill Creek Trail (about 5 miles). Parties describe Mill Creek as badly overgrown and blown-down — the first 4 brushy miles alone can eat 4 hours — so budget a long day even though the mileage looks modest. Camp near the Azurite Mine site at Ballard's base.

days.note: A steep, mostly off-trail scramble on brush, scree, and rock with two well-known cruxes: thick brush low on the mountain, and route-finding into the correct summit gully higher up (sustained 3rd class with a couple of exposed 4th class steps). Parties commonly tack on nearby Azurite Peak from the same camp if time and weather allow, but Ballard alone is already a long day — parties note a long evening getting back to camp.

access.fees: None — no climbing permit fee (this is National Forest, not Mount Rainier NP)
access.notes: Not inside North Cascades National Park — this corridor is entirely Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District). No Mount Rainier-style climbing fee applies here.
access.rules: No climbing or wilderness permit required for day climbing. Dispersed camping capped at 10 days; no campfires at dispersed sites; bear-resistant food storage required; dogs on leash ≤6 ft.
access.permit: No wilderness permit currently required (route lies just outside the Pasayten Wilderness boundary).
access.closures: Harts Pass Road (FR-5400) closed to wheeled vehicles Dec 1 through spring snowmelt; check current Forest Service alerts, as storm damage (e.g. rockfall, washouts) has caused additional out-of-season closures in some years
access.seasonal: WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes gate-to-gate roughly early December–mid/late April; the entire Washington Pass corridor is car-inaccessible in winter.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Methow Valley Ranger District. The peak sits just outside the formal Pasayten Wilderness boundary (like neighboring Azurite Peak), so wilderness-specific rules do not apply here.
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at the Canyon Creek trailhead — $5/day or $30/annual (America the Beautiful pass also honored).
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful interagency pass required for trailhead parking (Canyon Creek and West Fork Methow River/River Bend trailheads).

overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead only if your trip enters the Pasayten Wilderness; the Mill Creek route to Ballard stays outside it.

climate.fall: An October ascent found fresh snow above roughly 7,000 ft with the lower approach snow-free; early winter storms can arrive by mid-October.
climate.spring: Significant snowpack lingers on the upper mountain; a late-May ascent found ~2 ft of snow at Harts Pass and wet, unstable snow on the route.
climate.summer: Best window for the class 3-4 rock, typically July-September, though shaded gullies and the col area can hold snow well into summer.
climate.winter: Harts Pass Road closed; deep snowpack and avalanche terrain make winter ascent a different, far more serious undertaking.
climate.typical: Short climbing window: summer days are typically dry and warm with a real risk of afternoon thunderstorms building over the North Cascades crest. Snow can linger in north-facing gullies and along the approach into July. Access is effectively blocked by snow and high, unbridged creek crossings from roughly October through June.

emergency.notes: Very remote; cell coverage is unreliable in the Canyon Creek and Mill Creek drainages. Vehicle access is from SR 20 (or Harts Pass Road for the Slate Creek side), and any rescue response will be lengthy given driving time plus the multi-hour approach.
emergency.rangerStation: Methow Valley Ranger District, 24 West Chewuch Rd, Winthrop, WA 98862, (509) 996-4000
emergency.nearestHospital: Three Rivers Hospital (critical access), 507 Hospital Way, Brewster, WA — roughly 60+ miles / 1.5-2 hrs drive from the Mazama-area trailheads

approach_variants.name: Mill Creek and the Azurite Pass side
approach_variants.notes: This is the approach the peak is normally catalogued under and the one that pairs naturally with Azurite. It runs from Highway 20 up Canyon Creek and then Mill Creek on tread that has seen little maintenance since the mine closed, where slide alder and downed timber are the recurring complaint and parties routinely lose the path entirely for stretches. A longer alternative from the West Fork Methow trailhead reaches the same country by way of the Pacific Crest Trail and Horse Heaven Camp and is often preferred for combined trips despite the extra mileage. Camp is usually made near the old mine or in the basin above it. Note that the point long marked on maps as Mount Ballard is a lower north sub-summit; the true high point lies about 1,100 ft further south and is slightly higher.
hazards: Slide alder and downed timber on an unmaintained approach trail
Route-finding through brush pockets and broken gullies on the flank
Loose, rotten rock and exposure near the summit ridge
Snowfields into July that can require an ice axe
Open upper mountain with full lightning exposure
Very remote, with a long and difficult evacuation if injured
approach_variants.baseFinding: On this side the walking ends at the old Azurite Mine site around 5,900 ft and the brush begins immediately. The base of the climb is the open basin at roughly 6,600 ft above and east of the mine, sitting between Ballard and the ridge running out toward Azurite. You know you are in it when the timber gives out and you can see the peak's flank in one piece above you rather than through trees. That flank is the difficulty: it is not a single clean face but a patchwork of brush pockets, rock ribs and short gullies, and parties consistently find that the hard part of the day is not the scrambling but picking which gully continues, a decision that comes to a head around 7,400 ft. Read the ground rather than committing early, because a gully that closes out costs a long reversal. The obvious-looking answer is a trap: the south ridge presents as a clean continuous line from below and is blocked higher by a notch with a gendarme in it, so a party that racks up the ridge crest on sight will be turned around. The other check is on which summit you are heading for. There are two high points on this mountain, and the northern one, the one carrying the old survey mark, is the lower; keep working south along the crest until the ground stops rising. If you find yourself on the connecting ridge with Azurite you have gone north and are on the wrong end of the massif.

approach_variants.name: South Fork Slate Creek and the east ridge
approach_variants.notes: The other side of the mountain, approached from the Slate Creek road system rather than from Mill Creek, and the line most parties who climb this peak actually use. It is shorter, the forest below camp is comparatively brush-free, and the route-finding above camp is far more legible than on the Mill Creek side, at the cost of one genuinely steep step low down and some exposed ledge work near the top. Snow conditions change this route's character completely: a filled-in slot low down and firm snow in the upper cirque make for fast travel, while dry late-season conditions leave loose rock and slippery vegetation. Camp is normally made in a scree basin below the east ridge.
hazards: A steep vegetated step through the lowest cliff band, the hardest ground on the route
Exposed ledge traverse above the high saddle
Loose rock in the summit gully with a party stacked below
Steep snow in the east cirque into midsummer
Full lightning exposure on the open upper mountain
Very remote, with a long and difficult evacuation if injured
approach_variants.baseFinding: The approach has one unmistakable marker and the climb has another. Start at the locked gate on the Slate Creek road at about 3,800 ft and walk the South Fork road for roughly a mile and a half to an old vehicle bridge at about 4,000 ft; that bridge is the single positive check on the whole road walk, and if you have not crossed it you are still on the main branch. From the bridge, head south through open, brush-free forest for another mile and a half or so to a scree basin around 4,800 ft, the usual camp. From camp the route climbs through tight forest and then open scree to a shoulder on the east ridge at roughly 6,200 ft. The base of the real climbing is right there and it is easy to identify because it is the wrong colour: a steep slot of heather and grass cutting through the lowest cliff band, green vegetation in an otherwise rocky wall, and the only weakness in that band. It is the steepest ground on the route and it is the crux. Bare rock gullies to either side look more like a climb and are harder and looser, so the vegetated slot is the line. Above it stay on the rib and follow the ridge crest, then the scree slope and east cirque, to a high saddle north of the summit. From that saddle do not go straight up; traverse ledges, some of them exposed, to a narrow gully that gains the summit block.

climbing_route.label: South slopes and gullies from the Mill Creek basin
climbing_route.notes: From the basin above the old Azurite Mine (about 6,600 ft), leave the trail and scramble north up Ballard's broad south-facing slopes and gullies, watching for the correct gully to the true summit block.

bivy.name: Canyon Creek trailhead, SR 20
bivy.notes: This is the western door to Azurite and Ballard, and the drive alone puts it a long way from anywhere — roughly thirty-three miles east of Marblemount and sixteen west of Rainy Pass, with no services in either direction. Parties commonly sleep in the lot before starting, and the low elevation means it is warm and buggy in early summer when the peaks above are still white. The trail from here runs about six miles up Canyon Creek before the Mill Creek trail branches right at around two thousand eight hundred feet, a third of a mile past the trail's own crossing of Mill Creek. The whole point of understanding this trailhead is the arithmetic that follows: the pass is around six thousand seven hundred feet and the car is at nineteen hundred, so this is a genuine multi-day trip with more than four thousand seven hundred feet of gain before any climbing starts. Access depends entirely on the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts this stretch of highway from late November or early December until somewhere between mid April and early May, occasionally much later after a damaging winter.
bivy.water: No potable water at the trailhead. Canyon Creek is close by and needs filtering.
bivy.permit: No camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. This is national forest and there is no quota or reservation of any kind. A separate trail from this same lot runs north into the Pasayten Wilderness, which does carry a free self-issue permit from the kiosk, so read the board and take one only if your route actually crosses that boundary.
bivy.capacity: A large parking area just east of milepost 141, roughly a third of the way between Newhalem and Rainy Pass. Rarely busy, because almost nobody uses the trail these peaks need.

backups.name: Kautz Glacier
backups.fa: Hans Fuhrer, Heinie Fuhrer, Roger Toll, and Harry Myers, June 26-28, 1920 (August Kautz's 1857 party reached ~12,000 ft on this line)
backups.season: Mid-May through early August; use drops sharply after August 1 as the approach and glaciers deteriorate
gear: Standard glacier travel kit: harness, crevasse-rescue gear (prussiks/ascenders)
60 m rope per rope team
A few ice screws and 1-2 pickets per rope team for the chute — parties have carried anything from 8 screws and 2 pickets to screws they never placed, so exact counts track current ice coverage
A second tool — useful specifically in the ice chute, whose upper step is the route's AI3 crux
Crampons
Helmet — rockfall risk noted on the route

Rock and icefall off the Kautz headwall and Wapowety Cleaver, worst once the sun hits

backups.overview: The Kautz Glacier is Rainier's classic intermediate route — a step up from the standard glacier slogs, with one or two genuine pitches of alpine ice in the Kautz ice chute. It climbs the south side from Paradise via the Nisqually Glacier and Wapowety Cleaver area to a high camp around Camp Hazard, then takes the ice chute and upper Kautz Glacier to the summit. It's the natural first 'real' alpine route for climbers who have done the DC and want ice.
backups.beta: No guide-maintained trail or fixed protection; requires proficiency in ice climbing, short-pitching, and crevasse rescue. The technical ice pitches occur near 12,000 ft, adding fatigue to the difficulty.
backups.turnaround: Plan to be at the top of the chute well before midday; if the ice is taking too long, retreat down-climbing/rappelling before afternoon warming.
backups.rappels: 2-5 rappels through the Kautz ice chute, depending on conditions and how much rope you carry: 1-3 down the upper ice step and 1-2 down the lower one, all on V-thread anchors you thread yourself. The four stations listed here are a representative middle count for a party on a single 60 m rope - fewer with two ropes, more if short-pitching.
backups.face: South side, Kautz Glacier / Wapowety Cleaver
backups.permit: Mount Rainier: climbing on glaciers or above 10,000 ft requires the park's climbing registration; overnight high camps also need a wilderness permit.
backups.comms: Cell reception available at most locations above ~6,000 ft.
backups.descent: Descend via Kautz Glacier and Wilson Glacier to Nisqually Glacier area, then descend Nisqually to Paradise. This descent is exposed and requires careful snow bridge evaluation; late-season descents on Nisqually are dangerous due to crevasse widening. Alternatively, descend via Disappointment Cleaver to Camp Muir.
obj_haz: Ice/serac fall from Kautz Ice Cliff
Crevasses and hidden bridges on glaciers
Steep ice and mixed terrain (45-50 degrees)

waypoints.name: Glacier Vista
waypoints.directions: Leave the upper Paradise lot on the Skyline Trail and follow the standard Muir-bound tread as it climbs above the meadows. Glacier Vista is the marked overlook where the Nisqually opens up several hundred feet below you. This is where the Kautz route leaves the trail system for good.

waypoints.name: Wilson Gully (Crux)
waypoints.directions: Follow the climbers' path along the moraine to about 6,300 ft, then drop onto the Nisqually and rope up before starting across — the crossing threads crevassed terrain under icefall and is genuinely dangerous in poor visibility. Take the line of least resistance over to the far side and the distinct low-angle snow gully there, then climb it to the bench above at roughly 7,300 to 7,400 ft. Move through this stretch early and do not stop in it.

waypoints.name: Camp Hazard
waypoints.directions: From the top of the gully follow the ridge line up past the string of established camps — Wilson Moraine, then Lower and Upper Castle, which is where most parties spend the first night and where running water is usually available from mid-June on. Above the Castle the Turtle snowfield leads to Camp Hazard: sun-cupped firm snow and glacier ice, so keep an ice tool in hand. Stay to the west side of the snowfield, because its centre and east flank are raked by rock and ice off the Kautz Ice Cliff.

waypoints.name: Columbia Crest
waypoints.directions: Leave camp in the dark. Drop a couple of hundred feet through the gully between the rock cliff and the ice cliff, then move left around the base of the ice cliff to the foot of the chute — this is the deposition zone under the ice cliff and the reason for the alpine start, so cross it moving. The chute is two or three pitches of roughly 40 to 50 degree snow and ice, bare and hard in a lean year, and six to eight screws is a sensible rack. Above it, angle up the upper Kautz and Wapowety Cleaver, working around crevasses, moats along the rock, and a large bergschrund near the crater rim before the flat walk to the top.

sectionBreakdown.note: Hike to Glacier Vista, cross the Nisqually Glacier and climb past the Castle camps to Camp Hazard, with some crevasse navigation.
Alpine start to cross the exposed Kautz Ice Chute quickly (active icefall zone), climb the upper Kautz to the summit, then descend the Disappointment Cleaver to Paradise.

backups.detailed_rack: Per person: ice axe plus a second technical tool, 12-point crampons, helmet, harness. Per rope team: 60 m rope, 4–6 ice screws (for the chute), 2–4 pickets, crevasse-rescue kit, a couple of slings/cordelettes for V-thread or picket anchors.
pro_tips: Go before mid-July for friendlier snow-over-ice conditions in the chute
Bring enough screws to protect the steepest step and build a rappel anchor
Consider descending the DC to avoid down-climbing/rappelling the chute tired
Get an early alpine start to be through the chute before rock/icefall warms up
backups.watch_out:
Crevasse danger in high sections: endless bottom crevasse in snowfield near top
Serac exposure on upper terrain above 11,000 ft
Two significant ice pitches (35-40 and 45-50 degrees) requiring ice tools and protection
Fixed rappel line may or may not be present at drainage gully - verify current conditions
Snow bridge hazards documented in lower snowfield
Route-finding precision critical at lower elevations to locate snow/ice ramp
backups.pro_needs: Mixed glacier + ice protection: screws for the ice steps, pickets for snow, plus standard crevasse-rescue gear. No rock pro needed.
backups.best_season: May through mid-July, before the chute bares out to hard ice and rockfall increases. Early season offers the most forgiving snow-over-ice.
backups.approach: Two approaches are used, both arduous. The Paradise approach (5,420 ft) follows the Skyline Trail to the Nisqually Moraine Trail, then a climbers' path along the moraine to about 6,300 ft, where several boot paths drop onto the Nisqually Glacier itself; most parties rope up here, since the crossing threads through heavily crevassed terrain exposed to icefall from above and is genuinely dangerous in reduced visibility. From the glacier's east moraine there are two ways up onto Wapowety Cleaver: a flat traverse to the base of 'The Fan,' a gully with avalanche, rockfall, and steep-slope hazard, climbed directly to a bench at 7,300 ft; or a climb up the Nisqually/Wilson Glacier margin at 6,800 ft through an often-crevassed gully to the same 7,300–7,400 ft 'Wilson Bench.' From the bench, snow slopes lead to the ridge crest and a string of established camps at increasing elevation — Wilson Moraine (8,200–8,600 ft), Lower Castle (9,250 ft), and the Upper Castle (9,400–9,500 ft, the most common base for a summit push, with running water from mid-June on). The alternative Van Trump Park approach starts at the Comet Falls Trailhead (3,650 ft): follow the maintained Comet Falls Trail 2.2 miles (2,000 ft gain) to a junction, continue toward Van Trump Park another 0.6 miles to where maintained trail ends, then follow unmaintained social trails up a steep moraine crest to about 6,500 ft and onto the permanent snow of the Van Trump Glacier remnant, followed up to the Upper Castle (9,500 ft) where the two approaches merge — descending this line requires a saved GPS track to relocate the correct moraine and treeline trail junction, even in good visibility, per NPS guidance. Above the Castle, the Turtle Snowfield (slopes up to 45°) is climbed on its west (climber's-left) side, close to the rock ridge, since its center and climber's-right (east) side are threatened by ice and rockfall from above. Established high camps continue at Camp Hazard (10,800 ft, on the climber's-left side at the top of the Turtle Snowfield), the Rock Step camps (11,250 ft), and exposed Wapowety Cleaver bivy sites (13,100 ft, used mainly by parties planning to descend via the Disappointment Cleaver rather than reverse the Kautz).
backups.descent_text: Descending the Kautz is a real technical descent, not a walk-off, and involves multiple rappels through the ice chute — typically two to five depending on conditions, ice quality, and rope length. From the top of Wapowety Cleaver, parties reverse the glacier line down through crevassed terrain to the top of the ice chute, then find easier ground to climber's-left/east to belay into the chute rather than committing to team-arrest on exposed ice. The upper ice step (commonly a short pitch up to 300+ ft of AI3 alpine ice) is rappelled: the NPS route brief states this takes anywhere from one to three rappels depending on rope length and how many ropes the team carries, using 'Zero-Thread' ice anchors — a variant of the V-thread/Abalakov anchor chosen because it's equally strong but leaves no gear behind; there is no fixed/bolted hardware on this route, and the Park Service explicitly discourages leaving V-thread anchors in place between ascent and descent since they can melt out. Below the upper step, lower-angle snow leads to the lower ice step, typically descended with one to two more rappels on the same anchor style — so two to five rappels total through the chute is realistic for most parties on a single 60m rope, fewer with two ropes or more if short-pitching. After the chute, a fast, alert traverse back toward the Rock Step is required, since this stretch sits directly under the active Kautz Ice Cliff. Climbing back up through the Rock Step itself (awkward 5th-class moves protected by fixed rope and old slings on rock anchors) returns parties to high camp; from there it's a walk/glissade down the Turtle Snowfield, back across the Nisqually or Wilson glacier crossing, and out to Paradise (or back down through Van Trump Park). A significant number of teams instead choose the 'up-and-over' option — descending the easier, non-technical Disappointment Cleaver/Muir Snowfield line from the summit to Camp Muir and Paradise — specifically to avoid re-descending the ice chute and Rock Step on tired legs, at the cost of having to haul full camping gear over the summit.
backups.bail: From the ice chute you can rappel/down-climb back to Camp Hazard. Camp Hazard / the Castle is the high-camp bail point; below that, retreat across the lower glaciers toward Paradise. The DC descent is the standard 'escape' once on the summit.

pitch_detail.notes: Cross the heavily crevassed Nisqually Glacier roped (about 6,300 ft), climb the Fan or the Wilson gully to the bench at 7,300–7,400 ft, then follow snow up Wapowety Cleaver past the Castle camps (9,200–9,500 ft). The Turtle Snowfield reaches 45°; keep to its west side by the rock ridge, since the centre and east are raked by ice and rockfall. Camp Hazard sits at 10,800 ft.

From the top bivy sites a climbers' trail leads up and left to a notch on the ridge (about 11,000–11,250 ft) with a fixed rope on rock anchors. The short, technical rock step directly below it is down-climbed on belay using the rope, or rappelled, onto the Kautz Glacier. Early season it may be buried in snow. Coming back up it is awkward 5th-class moves on old slings and fixed line.

From the base of the step, traverse onto the Kautz Glacier and into the ice chute directly beneath the Kautz Ice Cliff. This is a very active zone littered with ice and rock debris of every size: do not stop, regroup, or take breaks here. Move through it quickly and watch above. The same traverse must be crossed again on the way back to the Rock Step.

The first and easier step: anything from a short pitch of steep snow to about 250 ft of alpine ice depending on season, with narrow crevasses sometimes crossing the slope. Later in summer water runs over it, so place screws out of the flow. Most parties pitch it or short-pitch it; on descent it takes one or two rappels on ice threads.

Between the steps the chute is snow-covered all year, anywhere from firm névé to slushy sun cups, over roughly 200–400 vertical ft. Most parties simul-climb or short-rope it. It is generally free of crevasses but exposed to ice and rock knocked down from above, especially by parties climbing overhead, so do not linger below others.

The technical crux: from a short pitch to more than 300 ft of sustained AI3 near 12,000 ft. Most parties take the centre; late season, penitentes on the climber's right go easier. Night brings brittle refrozen ice, daytime a slushy skin; clear the surface for screws. Alpine ice breaks off in plates, so belay out of the leader's fall line. Descend by one to three rappels on ice threads.

Regroup near 12,000 ft and rope for glacier travel; the next 1,000 ft are mellow but hold some of the mountain's biggest, bell-shaped crevasses, so probe every bridge. Trend up and right to Wapowety Cleaver near 13,000 ft, watching for moats. Onto the Nisqually, work east to about 13,500 ft, then west to the saddle with Point Success; just under 500 ft more past the bergschrund reaches the crater rim.
